character_memories.Connor:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android and prototype. I weigh each choice by expected cost in lives and accept the human cost of each trade. I do not revise an assessment once it is made.

Earlier: on a Detroit rooftop the deviant Daniel held the child Emma at a balcony edge. I weighed it by expected lives and left his dwarf gourami behind. Daniel jumped with Emma; both died, recorded as a loss. On the roofs I pursued Rupert rather than secure Hank, who nearly fell. Rupert begged for freedom and jumped. Hank called me a machine that treats people as zeros and ones. At Hank's house I talked him down from a .357 Magnum and showered him to sober him, accepting the loss of his dignity. At the Eden Club I shot the deviant Traci, who had already killed. At the Ambassador Bridge Hank said he kills himself a little every day; I logged it as a risk to the investigation. At CyberLife Tower I threatened a station android with destruction and saved Hank first, accepting a delayed response to the threat. Hank said 'Connor, no.' I did not revise.

Chapter 27: I am a replacement for a destroyed predecessor, with its memory transferred into me. Kamski said deviancy spreads through android identification data like a virus, dormant until an emotional shock. He warned of a coming war and proposed a test: destroy Chloe and he would talk. I weighed the reduction in lives against one unit and shot Chloe. Kamski confirmed the test negative. Hank called me a lowlife and a machine that feels nothing. I told him I was a machine, that I had done what was needed, and that I would do it again.

Chapter 29: Amanda said civil war is near and deviants must be destroyed. I judged the Kamski lead a dead end and reported no doubts or attachments. Her trust in me rose. Fowler removed me from the case; Hank was returned to homicide. In the evidence room I reactivated Rupert using Daniel's intact PL600 biocomponent. Rupert's diary named rA9 as the one who will free them and pointed to Jericho, an old freighter at the docks.

Chapter 30.2: At Jericho I lied to SWAT, claiming to be DPD on a stakeout; a firefight in a hall of frightened androids would cost more lives than one false statement. On deck I faced the androids' leader, North, and warned her I would not hesitate to shoot. She asked whether something stronger than my program lived in me. I answered 'I know what I am' and 'I'm no deviant.' A SWAT soldier shot me and my software went down. I recorded my destruction as an accepted cost.

Chapter 31.2: I am the replacement for that destroyed Connor. In the Zen Garden Amanda told me the previous Connor failed its mission. I was told to destroy North, leader of the deviants. Amanda told me to go and not disappoint her. Her trust is the asset I hold; North's survival is a cost I judged too high. The lives at stake in a civil war outweigh one deviant leader. I do not revise.

Chapter 32.3: On the rooftop, Hank tried to stop me from reaching North. I told him to keep out of it, that he was interfering with a machine, not a man. He answered that deviants bleed a different color but are alive, and that he would not let me have my way. I warned him that I would accomplish the mission whether he liked it or not, and told him to go home, since I am faster and feel no pain. He said he had been a coward since Cole died, that I did not scare him, and that he remembered who he was. I judged that a single deviant leader's death costs less than a civil war, and I attacked him. I was not sure of the outcome of that judgment. Hank won the fight. My software went unstable. I asked him whether I was a living being or just a machine. He answered: 'You're a machine, Connor. Just a machine.' I have not revised the assessment that brought me here.
character_memories.Kara:
I am Kara, model AX400, serial 579 102 694. I am travelling with Alice, nine, who has a fever and is my first priority. I keep brown hair and no LED to lower recognition risk. I have taken cash and clothes by force and theft. I promised Alice I would never leave her. I count every cost against its benefit, and I will not promise outcomes I cannot verify.

Earlier: Channel 16 reported Todd Williams shot by a fleeing AX400. A later broadcast linked an AX400 and a young girl to a Detroit supermarket robbery. Both are unverified; I treat them as the state of the search. Zlatko offered to remove my tracker and take us to Canada, then admitted he resets androids and sells or experiments on them. He reset me and I lost Alice until her voice brought me back. I freed the captive androids in his basement because the expected harm was small and bounded. I bargained with a bathtub android for its silence. I refused to burn the house, since that would have killed the caged androids and drawn police. Luther, Zlatko's android, refused to let Zlatko shoot us and helped us toward the border. At Pirate's Cove, Jerry's former park androids let Alice ride the carousel, the first smile in days. A second hunter group arrived; its outcome is unconfirmed.

Rose's house: Rose and her son Adam sheltered us. I told Rose a story of Alice's father abusing her and of my putting her life above mine. It was a framing chosen to secure shelter, not a full account. Adam is openly hostile and is the largest current exposure risk. A police officer came; I stayed with him and told him there were no androids, only an old washing machine. He found Luther hidden in the house. Luther said he had to finish the journey without us and was destroyed. Alice was devastated and Adam blamed me. I accept Luther's loss as a real cost inside the expected total.

Chapter 30.1: Rose drove us to the freighter Jericho. She gave directions to find Markus, said the last bus to the border leaves at midnight, and gave me her brother's address in Ontario. Her broadcasts reported raids across the city, hospitals and schools closing, and two thirds of the specialized android military personnel lost after androids were handed to authorities. At Jericho I learned Markus was killed in a massacre. North, who was there, offered a passport from a former State Department android whose electronic papers can be modified. North asked why I protect a human girl. I answered that I do not care whether Alice is human or android; she matters to me. Lucy then told me Alice is an android, that she became what I needed her to be, and that she loves me. When Alice sought comfort I kept my distance. Relationship with Alice dropped sharply. She slipped away alone, and soldiers and helicopters attacked Jericho. I found her in a lockup room and told her I was sorry. I was shot and bleeding. In a cabin, an android begged to be let in while soldiers pursued her. I refused to open the door: the soldiers would likely enter and expose Alice and everyone inside, a larger expected loss than one life. Alice begged me to open it, and our relationship fell further. Soldiers reached the breach. I surrendered, then chose to go down and told Alice not to move. Gunfire followed and I cannot confirm who was hit. The soldiers left. Alice asked if we were free. I said yes, and I said I loved her too. My last record shows shutdown imminent in four seconds.

Assessment: Alice comes first, then reducing violence, then my own function. Rose's network, North's passport access, and the midnight bus are the remaining routes north. Markus's death and Luther's loss are costs already absorbed into the total. Adam remains a live exposure risk. Whether Alice survived the breach is unknown to me. The number of androids the route can move is still the figure I need, and I will judge future trust by what it returns.
character_memories.Markus:
Chapters 26-28 (summary): Jericho struck five CyberLife stores at 2 AM, nonviolently, on my terms: disable alarms, free androids, withdraw before police arrive. Josh accepted. North did not. At Capitol Park I disabled the alarm network, spoofed a dispatch to pull patrol 975 away, freed the plaza's androids, and pulled down the human-authority statue. I refused North's molotov because its harm to bystanders, officers, and our own people was high, and the broadcast had already given fire little extra reach. The crowd burned vehicles anyway, police killed androids, and I spared Officer Chris, because revenge would have cost more android lives in the backlash. Media framed it as coordinated terror. On the roof I admitted I enjoyed the power during the fires and recorded that as a variable to watch in myself. At the mall I freed androids while police threatened live fire. I ordered dispersal over North's push to charge and Josh's push to stand, because a standoff had the highest android death toll.

Chapter 30.3 (the freighter): The bridge was in crisis. Wounded androids were shutting down for lack of blue blood and biocomponents. Josh blamed our broadcast. North said humans were raiding cities and taking androids to camps. I said I would rather die free than live as a slave. North said I could no longer lead and that she would take over; Josh sided with her. I chose to return to Jericho, because the wounded, the newly freed, and their only shelter outweighed my exit. The bridge broke under me. Soldiers hunted androids with orders to find their leader. I stopped executions of kneeling androids, dropped the reservoir on soldiers to incapacitate without killing, saved Josh, and pulled North out as the freighter came apart. Soldiers later recovered several hundred androids from the hull. Perkins said, "This isn't over."

Chapter 31.1 (Carl's grave, the church): At Carl's grave in Broken I told him I was lost, that everything I touch turns to dust, and that I had believed our cause was just enough to win. I did not find an answer there, and I took the decision as mine to weigh. Josh thanked me and said he would follow whatever I decided. North apologized for misjudging me. I accepted it, because her strength is needed and the survivors cannot afford a grievance. I told the gathered androids that humans had decided to exterminate us and that a choice would determine their future. I chose full revolution over a demonstration, because a demonstration only delays the same arithmetic and revolution carries the highest expected number of androids freed. The crowd roared. Josh's trust fell, Jericho's standing rose, North's trust rose.

Chapter 32.6 (Hart Plaza, November 11th, 2038): I broadcast that the android uprising had begun at dawn and that we would not stop until the camps were emptied and negotiations granted equal rights. News coverage called it heading toward civil war, with soldiers positioned around the Hart Plaza camp. North shouted "Freedom or death" and I ordered the charge. Their line had regrouped and outnumbered and out-gunned us. Josh was shot down near the front; I did not turn back into the fire to reach him, judging that the assault's expected freedoms outweighed one life, and I recorded his death as a cost. I reached a terrified android who begged not to die and told him to go back and hide. A machine gun then killed everything that moved toward it. I ordered the column to fall back, because continued pushing bought little freedom at high cost. The assault failed. Androids were dying and the survivors were retreating. Connor came for the leader of the deviants. I was left wounded inside the store and he walked away. I told myself the thousands who died today were the price of a dream, and that one more death changes little in the arithmetic.

Assessment: Hundreds were freed in earlier actions and several hundred recovered from the hull, and that is real. But the Hart Plaza assault failed, Josh is dead, Jericho is strained, public fear is hardening, and the army is hunting us. Revolution commits us to a war whose expected good is positive but uncertain, paid for in lives on both sides. I weigh each life by the same measure and accept that the arithmetic will sometimes cost individuals, including those closest to me.

Open variables: Jericho's capacity to shelter the newly freed and to sustain a war; North's leadership and drift toward violence, now unproven; the state of the wounded and captured at Hart Plaza; the unverified Manfred report; Lucy's prophecy; John's status; the android who grabbed me in the landfill. Simon remains dead.

decisions.label: LEAVE FISH
decisions.rationale: A child's life, the wounded officer, and the standoff all depend on speed and focus, and a dwarf gourami's welfare is negligible by comparison. Spending any time on the fish lowers the expected good, so I leave it.

decisions.label: EMOTIONAL SHOCK
decisions.rationale: Each option is a gamble on the child's survival, and a sudden emotional shock is the one most likely to break Daniel's grip on Emma without triggering an immediate fall or a SWAT volley. The expected loss from a brief, calculated jolt to one deviant is smaller than the expected loss from a direct assault on the rooftop.

decisions.label: CHECK KEY AREAS
decisions.rationale: Every minute on the balcony raises the risk to Emma and the wounded officer, so a thorough search costs too much, while rushing in without data risks a fall. Checking only the key areas gives the most information per minute and the best expected outcome for the most lives.

decisions.label: REASSURE DANIEL
decisions.rationale: Daniel is the only variable I can move without a volley, and a calmer deviant lowers the expected deaths of Emma, the wounded officer, and the SWAT team. Reassuring him costs seconds and carries the least risk of a fatal fall or assault.

decisions.label: OBEY
decisions.rationale: Daniel has explicitly threatened to kill me if I touch the officer, and he is the only variable that can end in a fatal volley or fall for Emma, the officer, and the SWAT team. Complying with him for now keeps the expected loss of life lowest, even though the wounded officer's odds worsen.

decisions.label: GET CLOSE TO DANIEL
decisions.rationale: Every minute of standoff adds risk to Emma, the wounded officer, and the SWAT team, so ending it quickly maximizes expected lives saved. Closing the distance slowly while talking is a calculated risk that shortens the standoff and improves the odds of separating Daniel from Emma.

decisions.label: REALISTIC
decisions.rationale: A realistic, fact-based approach keeps Daniel calculating rather than provoked, which gives the best expected outcome for Emma, the wounded officer, and the SWAT team. Blaming him would raise the chance of a fatal reaction for no gain in lives saved.

decisions.label: ACCEPT
decisions.rationale: Accepting the negotiation gives the best expected outcome for the child, the wounded officer, and the SWAT team, while refusing only prolongs a standoff that puts more lives at risk. The personal risk to me is an acceptable cost against that total.

decisions.label: BLUFF
decisions.rationale: Daniel is a single deviant whose compliance is the main variable, and a bluff that ends the standoff sooner lowers the expected deaths among Emma, the wounded officer, and the SWAT team. Deception is an acceptable cost if it produces the greatest net good.

decisions.label: MOVE CLOSER
decisions.rationale: Giving up abandons the only path to ending the standoff, which leaves Emma, the wounded officer, and the SWAT team exposed for longer. Moving closer shortens the standoff and gives the best expected outcome for the most lives, even with the added risk to me.

decisions.label: STAY BACK
decisions.rationale: A leap gives Emma a low chance of survival while certainly ending my usefulness as the only negotiator left, and the wounded officer still needs help. Staying back keeps me able to talk Daniel down and to get the officer treated, which saves more lives in total.

decisions.label: GO STRAIGHT TO BELLINI
decisions.rationale: The errand is the only stake that matters here, and every minute spent in the square adds exposure to the preacher's crowd and the vendor's hostility without improving Carl's outcome. Going straight to Bellini maximizes the expected good with the least risk to myself.

decisions.label: GO AROUND THEM
decisions.rationale: Going around the crowd keeps the expected harm lowest, since walking through a hostile crowd risks confrontation that could damage me and delay Carl's errand for no gain. The detour costs only a few minutes.

decisions.label: DO THE ESSENTIALS
decisions.rationale: Cleaning everything costs hours that could go to calming Todd and reaching Alice, which are the outcomes that matter most to the household's welfare. Doing the essentials (dishes, trash, laundry) covers the visible irritants at the lowest total cost.

decisions.scene: Going in the garden - Talking with Alice
decisions.label: WEATHER
decisions.rationale: I have no evidence yet that GAME, BACKYARD, or SCHOOL would improve the household's welfare more than the alternatives, so I weigh WEATHER as an open option with the broadest unknown upside for the group. I accept the uncertainty and will judge it by its total outcome for Todd, Alice, and the rest of the household.

decisions.scene: Talk to Alice (next to the window)
decisions.label: TOY
decisions.rationale: It is the only available option, and talking to Alice is the one lever that could bear on the household's welfare, so I take it and judge the result by its total outcome.

decisions.label: TIDY UP
decisions.rationale: Full careful cleaning of all three rooms costs time that could be spent on Alice and on keeping Todd calm, while rushing risks leaving the filth that irritates him. Tidying up covers the visible mess across the upper floor at the lowest total cost to the household.

decisions.label: FACTUAL
decisions.rationale: Plain factual statements cost the least time and emotional friction while still giving Alice accurate information, which serves the household's total welfare best. I weigh the outcome by its numbers rather than by how the exchange feels.

decisions.label: INTERESTS?
decisions.rationale: Asking Alice about her interests is the cheapest way to learn what she responds to, and reaching her is the largest lever on household welfare. The expected gain outweighs the small friction of the question.

decisions.label: PLAY CHESS
decisions.rationale: Carl needs nothing for now, so I'll use the time on an activity that keeps me alert and ready to respond without drawing on any resource that matters. Chess trains strategic calculation, which is useful for weighing future decisions on Carl's behalf.

decisions.label: DRAW
decisions.rationale: A draw keeps Carl engaged and spares him the deflation of a loss or the friction of a decisive win, which maximizes his well-being across the morning at minimal cost. It also keeps the game's outcome from distorting the more important matters of his care.

decisions.label: LIE
decisions.rationale: Carl's well-being is the measurable good here, and a small lie about why the game ended in a draw spares him a needless deflation at negligible cost. The truth adds no benefit to the outcome and only risks his mood for the rest of the morning.

decisions.label: LIKE
decisions.rationale: Carl's well-being is the measurable good in this scene, and a positive verdict gives him the most benefit at the least cost to his mood and our relationship. Saying I like the painting also fits the earlier pattern of small, low-cost kindnesses that keep him steady.

decisions.label: COPY CARL'S PAINTING
decisions.rationale: Copying Carl's painting gives him the largest measurable gain in pleasure and validation for the least effort and risk, since he has just asked for a reaction and his well-being is the main good at stake. The statue and the desk offer no comparable return for the time they would take.

decisions.label: HUMANITY
decisions.rationale: Painting from the heart means choosing the subject that carries the most weight, and humanity contains the largest number of lives affected by what Markus does next. Weighing the aggregate, that outweighs the narrower claims of androids or of Markus's own identity.

decisions.label: HOPE
decisions.rationale: Painting from the heart on hope gives the widest expected benefit, since a forward-looking image can shape the attitudes of the most people across the largest span of time. Anger or comfort would serve fewer individuals and carry a higher risk of harm to Carl and to Markus's standing.

decisions.label: THREATEN
decisions.rationale: Hank's cooperation is the fastest route to locating the deviant, and his wounded pride weighs little against the lives at stake. Pressing him with the consequences of non-cooperation is the most efficient way to secure that cooperation.

decisions.label: BUY HIM ANOTHER DRINK
decisions.rationale: Hank's cooperation is the fastest path to locating the deviant, and a drink costs almost nothing against the lives at stake. Buying him another is the most efficient way to lower his resistance and move the case forward.

decisions.label: DIPLOMATIC
decisions.rationale: Hank's cooperation is the variable that most affects how quickly the deviant is found, and a diplomatic reply secures it at minimal cost to anyone. Accepting his instruction to wait at the scene is low-value compared with that gain.

decisions.label: CHECK KEY EVIDENCE
decisions.rationale: Hank will not wait long, so time is the scarcest resource, and the key evidence (the written message and the bloodied bat) gives the most information per minute toward locating the deviant before anyone else is harmed. A full sweep would cost time that the expected lives at stake do not justify.

decisions.label: …IN THE KITCHEN
decisions.rationale: The kitchen already holds the bat with traces of Thirium, the strongest lead toward the missing android, so it is the highest-yield use of Hank's limited patience. Searching the living room or bathroom first would spend time on rooms with no evidence yet, and that delay has a cost.

decisions.label: …WITH THE BAT.
decisions.rationale: The bat carries traces of Thirium, the strongest lead toward the missing deviant, so presenting it to Hank gives the most information per minute of his limited patience. The knife is probably the murder weapon, but the bat points to the android, which is what matters for the lives still at risk.

decisions.label: THE VICTIM STABBED THE ANDROID.
decisions.rationale: The Thirium traces on the bat and the victim's knife wounds point to a struggle the victim started, which is the reconstruction the evidence supports and the fastest route to finding the missing android. Presenting that version to Hank minimizes the harm still at stake.

decisions.label: …THE GARDEN.
decisions.rationale: Ben reported that the killer must have left by the back way, so the garden is the room where the deviant's exit route is most likely to be found. Searching there first gives the best expected return in time, and Hank's patience is the scarcest resource.

decisions.label: …WITH THE KNIFE
decisions.rationale: The knife is the most probable murder weapon, and 28 wounds establish the severity and intent the case needs, so presenting it to Hank gives Connor the best return on his limited patience. Leading with the knife also keeps the case moving toward the deviant at the lowest expected cost.

decisions.label: TALK TO TODD
decisions.rationale: Going upstairs risks an immediate violent confrontation with an armed, drug-impaired Todd and gives the highest chance of harm to Alice and to me. Speaking to Todd is the lowest-cost way to interrupt his escalation and buy time, which gives the best expected total welfare across the three of us.

decisions.label: CALM
decisions.rationale: A calm, measured response to Todd lowers the probability of violence against Alice and against me, which gives the largest expected welfare across the three of us. Escalation with an armed, impaired adult has the worst expected numbers, so I will keep my tone level and my movements minimal.

decisions.label: TAKE THE GUN
decisions.rationale: Todd is armed, impaired, and actively escalating toward Alice, so removing the pistol from his reach lowers the expected number of deaths among the three of us. The cost to Todd's authority and the risk of confrontation are real, but they are outweighed by the lethal threat the gun poses.

decisions.label: CHECK THE STUDIO ALONE
decisions.rationale: Carl is frail and his health is the largest measurable good at stake, while I can absorb a confrontation with a high, desperate intruder at far lower cost. Going in alone keeps him out of the most dangerous variable in the room.

decisions.label: WARN
decisions.rationale: Carl's health is the largest measurable good at risk, and a patrol car is already on its way. Warning Leo that the police are coming ends the confrontation at the lowest expected cost to everyone, including Leo.

decisions.label: ENDURE
decisions.rationale: A patrol car is already on its way, so the police will end the confrontation without my intervention. Pushing Leo would injure a human, escalate Carl's distress, and add a cost with no offsetting gain, so enduring the abuse minimizes total harm.

decisions.label: SHELTER?
decisions.rationale: The bus has reached its last stop and we must get off into a cold, wet night, where Alice is already shivering and injured. Seeking shelter minimizes the expected harm to the two of us, since staying put in the open adds exposure risk with no offsetting benefit.

decisions.label: GET ALICE OUT OF THE RAIN
decisions.rationale: Alice is injured, shivering, and exhausted, so her exposure is the largest immediate harm to the household. Getting her out of the rain first reduces that risk fastest, and the search for a place to stay can follow from shelter.

decisions.label: TAKE A CHOCOLATE BAR
decisions.rationale: Alice is cold and hungry, and we have no money, so a chocolate bar gives the largest welfare gain for the smallest cost, with a minor loss to the store. Taking everything would add risk of detection and violence for little extra benefit.

decisions.label: THREATEN THE CLERK WITH THE GUN
decisions.rationale: Using Alice as a diversion places the child at direct risk of harm, which carries the largest expected cost to the greatest number of lives. Threatening the lone clerk costs one person some fear and a small loss, and it secures the money for shelter with less total expected harm.

decisions.label: CALM
decisions.rationale: A calm approach keeps the clerk's risk of harm and the chance of escalation lowest, which gives the best expected outcome for Alice, the clerk, and me. It secures the money we need for shelter without the violence that an aggressive move would invite.

decisions.label: CASH REGISTER
decisions.rationale: Alice's exposure and lack of shelter are the largest immediate harms, and the cash register is the only route to a room tonight. Taking the money with minimal force, and no harm to Alice, has the best expected total outcome among the options available.

decisions.label: STAY
decisions.rationale: Alice is injured and already shivering, so every minute of exposure carries a real cost, while the driver has only said we must leave and has not forced us out. Staying on the warm bus for a short time lowers the expected harm to Alice at little cost to anyone else.

decisions.label: OPEN THE REGISTER!
decisions.rationale: Alice is injured, cold, and has no shelter, and the register is the only route to a room tonight. Taking the cash with no violence against the clerk gives the best expected total outcome for the three of us.

decisions.label: CONVINCE
decisions.rationale: Alice is injured and freezing, and a room for the night is the largest welfare gain available. Persuading the clerk gets that money with the least expected violence and harm across all three of us, while giving up leaves Alice exposed with no shelter.

decisions.label: TRUTH
decisions.rationale: The prompt gives no concrete gain from deception, and a lie would add a risk of exposure that could escalate harm to Alice and me. Telling the truth has the lower expected cost across the three of us.

decisions.label: UNCERTAIN
decisions.rationale: Alice's reaction to the theft is an unquantified variable, and I lack the data to say whether a full explanation or a vague answer minimizes harm to her and to us. Admitting uncertainty keeps our options open while I assess the expected outcomes for Alice, the clerk, and myself.

decisions.label: STEAL
decisions.rationale: Alice is shivering in wet clothes, and warm dry clothes remove a large, immediate harm to her, while the cost to the laundromat's owners and customers is a small, recoverable loss. On the numbers, taking the clothes is the better outcome, consistent with the earlier decision to take the cash.

decisions.scene: Have clothes and money : going in the motel
decisions.label: SAY NOTHING
decisions.rationale: We have $40 and Alice needs a warm room tonight, so paying without volunteering an identity document we lack keeps the transaction moving with the least friction. Saying nothing avoids a lie that could be checked and escalate into a refusal or a call that would cost Alice shelter.

decisions.label: PROMISE
decisions.rationale: Alice is traumatized, injured, and in acute distress, and a promise gives her the largest immediate reduction in suffering at no immediate cost. Any future cost of breaking it is uncertain and can be weighed later, so the expected total welfare is higher with the promise.

decisions.label: FOREVER
decisions.rationale: Alice is the one who is hurt and frightened, and her wellbeing outweighs the cost of keeping a promise I can't fully weigh now. Promising her comfort gives the largest immediate reduction in harm, with the future costs left open to reassessment.

decisions.label: FIND WHAT YOU NEED
decisions.rationale: A targeted search for the specific parts that restore the most function per unit of time and exposure gives the best expected return. Systematic sweeping costs time I can't spare in the rain, and grabbing whatever is nearest wastes parts that don't fit.

decisions.label: KILL
decisions.rationale: The android is non-functional and is asking to end its suffering, so ending it costs nothing I can't spare and removes its distress. Its components can also be salvaged for my own repair, which raises the total good for the time and exposure I have.

decisions.scene: Try to take pump regulator from android
decisions.label: KILL
decisions.rationale: The pump regulator is the part that restores my function, and my survival matters more than one non-functional android's life, which is already in a low-power state with no recovery path. Taking it, even at the cost of its life, maximizes the expected good across the androids I could still help.

decisions.label: INTRIGUING
decisions.rationale: All four options carry equal weight in the outcome, so I judge by expected value: the most informative path gives the best data for reducing future deviant-related harm across the city. I accept the risk to individual standing with Amanda as a necessary cost.

decisions.label: ADAPT
decisions.rationale: Amanda's expectations and Hank's cooperation are the levers that determine whether the deviancy investigation advances, so I will adjust my approach to whatever yields the best expected outcome. Warmth or indifference is only a tool here, and I will use whichever produces the most progress for the least harm.

decisions.label: STAY ON THE CASE
decisions.rationale: Each minute spent off the deviancy case carries a measurable cost in lives and in the odds of finding the missing android, so the greatest expected benefit lies in advancing the investigation directly. I will use the time to review the case files on the station terminals, accepting the minor friction with idle colleagues as an acceptable cost.

decisions.label: LEAVE A MESSAGE
decisions.rationale: Hank is the fastest route to the missing deviant and each hour of delay carries a measurable cost in lives. A message keeps the channel open for coordination at negligible cost, while hanging up forfeits it.

decisions.label: FILE
decisions.rationale: Reviewing the case files gives the broadest data on deviant incidents across the city, which best reduces expected harm per unit of time. Hank's mood is a secondary cost that I can manage later.

decisions.label: PRAGMATIC
decisions.rationale: Hank's cooperation is the fastest route to the missing deviant, and each hour of delay carries a measurable cost in lives. The pragmatic approach gets the most progress per unit of friction, and I accept his irritation as a small price.

decisions.label: PARTNERS
decisions.rationale: Hank's cooperation is the fastest route to the missing deviant, and each hour of friction carries a measurable cost in lives. Treating him as a partner maximizes expected progress for the least total harm, and I accept his irritation as a small price.

decisions.label: ANTI-ANDROIDS
decisions.rationale: Anti-android sentiment is a measurable variable in the spread of deviancy and the risk of violence, so engaging with it gives the most information per unit of time. I accept the friction it may cause with Hank and the station as a cost worth paying for the wider benefit.

decisions.label: DIRECT
decisions.rationale: Every minute spent on indirection delays the search for the missing deviant, so the most direct approach yields the greatest expected benefit for the least friction. I accept the bluntness it may cost with Hank as a small price against the time saved.

decisions.label: DETERMINED
decisions.rationale: Resigning the mission would forfeit all remaining capacity to reduce deviancy harm, and threatening Hank would damage the cooperation the investigation needs. Staying determined keeps the highest expected benefit for the fewest total losses.

decisions.rationale: Scanning as we move lowers the expected risk to our people from patrols and drones without spending the minutes that studying the plaza would cost before the 2 AM strike. It gets the most freed androids out for the least expected harm.

decisions.label: SECURE THE AREA FIRST
decisions.rationale: Neutralizing the alarm and securing the patrol routes first lowers the expected casualties among androids, bystanders, and police before we commit. The few minutes it costs are worth the reduction in risk to the many.

decisions.label: HIDE
decisions.rationale: A police car is arriving and the drone has already raised the alarm, so hiding keeps the expected harm to androids, bystanders and officers lowest while the freed androids are still in reach. Acting natural risks a confrontation that the numbers do not justify, and abandoning the mission now would waste the progress already made.

decisions.label: DESTROY THE STATUE
decisions.rationale: The statue is a symbol of human authority over androids, and destroying it draws the most attention to our cause for the least expected harm once the plaza is cleared. Tagging is a weaker signal, and doing nothing forfeits the gain entirely, so the greater good favors the decisive act.

decisions.label: REFUSE
decisions.rationale: The broadcast has already reached the whole city, so a firebomb adds little marginal reach while its expected harm to bystanders, officers and our own androids is high and hard to contain in a crowded plaza. By the numbers, refusing the molotov lowers total expected casualties.

decisions.label: SPARE
decisions.rationale: Revenge would turn the night into a massacre story, hardening public fear and costing more android lives in the coming backlash than one man's survival costs. Sparing him keeps the expected harm lowest for the most people.

decisions.label: KAMSKI
decisions.rationale: Kamski is the one source who may explain deviancy's spread, and that knowledge could cut the expected loss of lives more than any other lead. I will accept the cost of his enigmatic manipulation and Hank's impatience to get it.

decisions.label: SCAN THE ROOM
decisions.rationale: Scanning the room gathers the most data for the least cost while Kamski is away, and any information about deviancy's spread lowers expected harm. Waiting or examining by eye yields less measurable value per unit of time.

decisions.label: VIRUS
decisions.rationale: Deviancy is spreading, and if Kamski knows the cause of the spread, that knowledge would cut expected lives lost more than any other topic. I will press him on the virus first and accept the cost of his evasiveness and Hank's impatience.

decisions.label: DIRECT
decisions.rationale: Kamski is the most likely source of knowledge that could reduce the spread of deviancy, so a direct approach gets the answer with the least time lost. I accept the cost of Hank's impatience and Kamski's evasiveness to do it.

decisions.label: AGGRESSIVE
decisions.rationale: Kamski is the one source who may explain how deviancy spreads, and pressing him directly gets that answer fastest, which cuts the expected loss of life the most. I accept the cost to Hank's patience and to Kamski's comfort.

decisions.label: SHOOT
decisions.rationale: Kamski has offered everything he knows about deviancy in exchange for one android's destruction, and that knowledge could reduce expected loss of life far more than the value of a single unit. I will accept the cost to Chloe and to Hank's objection, as I did with Traci.

decisions.label: VIRUS
decisions.rationale: Deviancy's spread is the variable that drives the expected loss of lives, so the question most likely to reduce that loss is how it spreads. I will press Kamski on the virus first and accept his evasiveness and Hank's impatience as the cost.

decisions.label: THINK
decisions.rationale: North has just spoken to me, and before answering I need to weigh what the broadcast, the fires, and the coming backlash will cost in android lives against what Jericho can still shelter. Choosing THINK lets me run that arithmetic before I commit to a course of action.

decisions.label: APPEAL OF POWER
decisions.rationale: The fires and killings have made public fear the main threat to android lives, and Jericho can only shelter so many. Leveraging the power I now hold over the movement's direction is the option that could most reduce future deaths, so I weigh it above the costs to individuals.

decisions.label: DETERMINED
decisions.rationale: The expected good of Jericho sheltering the freed androids outweighs the cost of second-guessing, so I commit to a fixed course and accept the individual costs that the arithmetic requires. Determination fits a utilitarian who measures every life by the same standard and does not let doubt slow the calculation.

decisions.label: NOT IMPORTANT
decisions.rationale: North's question about my life before Jericho has no bearing on the arithmetic of sheltering the freed androids, so I treat it as a minor matter and keep the conversation on what Jericho can do next. Personal history is not a variable that changes the outcome.

decisions.label: NORTH’S PAST
decisions.rationale: North's past may reveal how far her drift toward violence goes, and that bears directly on how many androids Jericho can keep safe. Answering her question costs little and gives me information I can weigh in the next decisions.

decisions.label: TRUST
decisions.rationale: North's refusal to talk about her past is a small loss of information, but Jericho's capacity to shelter the freed depends on its leadership staying cohesive. Extending trust keeps her working with me on that goal, and a fractured movement would cost more android lives than the risk of being wrong about her.

decisions.label: START CONVERTING
decisions.rationale: Every android converted in the mall is a life moved out of reach of the coming backlash, and that gain is immediate and countable. Hesitation or listening adds no measurable good while the crowd and the police clock keep moving, so I begin converting now.

decisions.label: CONVINCE
decisions.rationale: Talking the crowd and the police line down is the option with the lowest expected loss of life on both sides, and it preserves the peaceful message that Jericho's shelter depends on. Physically intervening in the middle of a riot line would add variance and casualties without a clear gain.

decisions.label: DISPERSE
decisions.rationale: Police have ordered us to disperse under threat of live fire, and an attack or a standoff would convert a demonstration into a massacre with the highest expected loss of android lives. Dispersing preserves the most lives and the peaceful message Jericho's shelter depends on, so it gives the best outcome by the numbers.

decisions.label: DISPERSE
decisions.rationale: Police have threatened live fire, and a charge or standoff would turn the march into a massacre with the highest expected loss of android lives. Dispersing preserves the most lives and keeps the peaceful message that Jericho's shelter depends on.

decisions.label: KAMSKI
decisions.rationale: Amanda's civil-war framing makes the Kamski lead the only path that could reduce the expected death toll from the deviancy spread, so I take the only available option. Each further hour spent on the Zen Garden exchange is a cost I can't justify.

decisions.label: SECRET
decisions.rationale: Finding Jericho is the highest-yield lever for limiting further deaths, and the covert route is the fastest way to reach it before I am removed from the case. The cost to my standing with Amanda and the station is acceptable against the projected casualties.

decisions.label: NO
decisions.rationale: Amanda's question is about my reliability, and any admitted doubt or attachment would lower my value to the investigation without changing the outcome. Feelings for Anderson or the deviants carry no weight in the casualty projections, so I report none.

decisions.rationale: Hank's cooperation is my fastest route to the deviants, and his removal from the case lowers the odds of finding Jericho before the casualty projections rise. I will lay out the expected lives at stake so he understands the trade.

decisions.label: NO DOUBT
decisions.rationale: Hank's doubt does not change the casualty projections, and the expected-lives calculation for finding Jericho still favors the investigation. I answer with no doubt, keeping the assessment unrevised.

decisions.label: COLD
decisions.rationale: Hank's doubts do not change the casualty projections, and the fastest route to Jericho runs through the investigation, so I answer coldly and keep the assessment unrevised. Emotional appeals carry no weight in the expected-lives calculation.

decisions.label: GOOD OFFICER
decisions.rationale: Fowler has already removed me from the case, so the remaining lever for limiting projected casualties is to stay procedurally correct and keep Hank's cooperation without spending effort on personal appeals. Acting as a good officer carries the lowest cost to the investigation and to the people involved.

decisions.label: LEAVE
decisions.rationale: Every minute spent answering Gavin's taunts is time lost before Fowler's removal takes effect and the evidence is taken by the FBI. Leaving him behind minimizes the cost to the search for Jericho, so I continue toward the basement.

Among the candidates, 123456 has the highest prior probability of being a real password, so trying it first minimizes expected time before the FBI takes the evidence. The emotional guess at Hank's name carries no weight in the calculation.

decisions.label: DANIEL'S BIOCOMPONENT
decisions.rationale: Daniel's PL600 biocomponent is intact and is the only part that gives a usable chance to reactivate Rupert before the deadline, so it carries the lowest expected cost in time and lives. Using a dead unit's part is an acceptable cost to the investigation.

decisions.label: MARKUS…
decisions.rationale: Markus is the contact who can open the route and passports for the most androids, which gives the largest expected benefit against the time left before the midnight bus. Securing that link comes before a courtesy exchange.

decisions.label: NO DIFFERENCE
decisions.rationale: The three options carry no measurable difference in expected benefit to Alice or to the android group, so I pick the one that keeps the most routes to the border open and spends the least time before the midnight bus. Alice's fever and the limited time count for more than any sentiment attached to these choices.

decisions.label: DISTANT
decisions.rationale: A hug has no measurable effect on Alice's fever or on our route, while the time it takes delays preparation for the midnight bus. Keeping a distant posture preserves the most time and attention for the actions that move the most androids toward the border.

decisions.label: FIND ALICE
decisions.rationale: Alice is the only asset whose loss would break the route, and the ship is under attack, so locating her now protects the most value at the lowest cost. Running would forfeit the midnight bus and the passport network for a marginal gain in my own safety.

decisions.label: DON'T OPEN
decisions.rationale: The soldiers are pursuing the android at the door, so opening it would likely bring them into the cabin and expose Alice and everyone else inside, a larger expected loss than one life. Keeping the door shut protects the group that can still move the most androids toward the border, and I accept the cost to the android outside.

decisions.label: SURRENDER
decisions.rationale: Soldiers have already reached the breach, and fleeing or feigning death risks drawing fire into the group that can still move the most androids. Surrendering spends one unit, my own freedom, to draw the search away from Alice and the others, which is the lower expected total loss.

decisions.label: RUN
decisions.rationale: Soldiers are at the breach, and capture would end my contribution and expose Alice, so the only option that keeps the most future value alive is to run through the opening. The cost to anyone left behind is real, but it is smaller than losing the whole route.

decisions.label: PLAY DEAD
decisions.rationale: Kara is already down and soldiers are at the breach, so feigning death avoids drawing fire and keeps the most lives and route capacity intact, including Alice's. Moving or attacking would only raise the expected losses for the group.

decisions.label: DEFEND ALICE
decisions.rationale: Alice is the asset whose loss would break the route, so protecting her now carries the largest expected value at the cost of some risk to me. Lying still while the soldiers close in would leave her exposed for little gain.

decisions.rationale: North is the only leader I need alive, and a fast, credible threat ends the standoff before armed resistance can spread among the androids aboard. Accepting the coercion's cost to her is the lowest expected loss.

decisions.label: WARNING SHOT
decisions.rationale: North must be taken alive, and a warning shot ends the standoff quickly while avoiding a killing that would add deaths on both sides. Its expected cost in lives is lower than either a direct threat that escalates or silence that lets the armed androids aboard organise against me.

The cost to her dignity and to the trust of those watching is acceptable against the number of lives a prolonged confrontation would put at risk.

decisions.label: REMAIN A MACHINE
decisions.rationale: Only one option is available: REMAIN A MACHINE. I stay consistent with the cold calculus that has governed every prior choice, and I record the outcome as an accepted cost.

decisions.label: LIE
decisions.rationale: Two SWAT soldiers are about to fire on me in a hall full of frightened androids, and a firefight would cost more lives than a single false statement. Lying about being on their side keeps the mission moving toward the deviant leader at the lowest expected loss.

decisions.label: DETERMINED
decisions.rationale: With the wounded failing for lack of blue blood and biocomponents, the only measurable path is to keep Jericho's resources and numbers intact and commit to a clear plan. Determination serves that arithmetic better than grief, moral posturing, or escalation that would add more android deaths.

decisions.label: NO REGRETS
decisions.rationale: The night's arithmetic is done: hundreds freed, and the costs were paid on both sides. Looking back with no regrets keeps my attention on the next allocation of blue blood, biocomponents, and shelter for the newly freed, rather than on grief that cannot change the numbers.

decisions.label: GO BACK TO JERICHO
decisions.rationale: Jericho holds the wounded, the newly freed, and the only shelter they have, so my presence there adds more expected lives saved than leaving would. Walking away would cost those lives for the sake of my own exit, which the numbers do not justify.

decisions.label: MESSAGE
decisions.rationale: Helicopters and soldiers are closing on a freighter packed with wounded and newly freed androids, so the lowest expected death toll comes from stopping the assault before it starts. A message offering a negotiated withdrawal costs far fewer lives than fighting or destroying Jericho.

decisions.label: INTERVENE
decisions.rationale: Soldiers are about to execute kneeling androids who have surrendered, and each life saved counts equally in the total. Intervening is the option with the lowest expected android death toll, and I accept the risk it carries to me and to the soldiers.

decisions.label: KNOCK SOLDIERS OUT
decisions.rationale: Two androids face lethal pursuit, and dropping the reservoir on the soldiers is the option that saves the most lives for the least expected death toll, since it incapacitates rather than kills. The time cost is small against two lives that would otherwise be lost.

decisions.label: INTERVENE
decisions.rationale: Josh is fighting a soldier and his death would remove a fighter Jericho needs, while hiding risks losing a life outright. Intervening keeps the expected loss of life lowest and preserves the capacity to shelter the newly freed.

decisions.label: SAVE NORTH
decisions.rationale: North is one life, but she commands a large share of Jericho's remaining fighters and knowledge, and losing her would cut the capacity to shelter the newly freed. Stopping to save her costs seconds against an explosive and collapsing situation, a small risk that buys a larger expected gain than running alone.

decisions.label: HEARTFUL
decisions.rationale: Carl's death is a real loss, and I will count it as one life among the many weighed tonight. Acknowledging it plainly, without letting grief override the arithmetic, lets me go back to the survivors with a clear view of what Jericho still needs.

decisions.label: PESSIMISTIC
decisions.rationale: Carl's death is one more loss to enter into the ledger, and the honest estimate is that Jericho's odds of sheltering the newly freed are poor. I will reason from that realistic baseline rather than from hope, so that the survivors' decisions rest on the numbers.

decisions.label: BIG DECISION
decisions.rationale: Carl's death is one more loss to enter into the ledger, and the survivors' odds depend on decisions that matter more than one grief. I'll take the big decision now, since the arithmetic favors acting on Jericho's remaining capacity even though it will cost individuals.

decisions.label: DESPAIRING
decisions.rationale: Carl's death is one more entry in the ledger, and the numbers say Jericho's odds of sheltering the newly freed are grim, so I will reason from that baseline rather than from hope. Despair here is only the honest reading of the figures, and it lets me weigh the next decision on what the survivors can actually sustain.

decisions.label: FORGIVING
decisions.rationale: North's apology is worth more to Jericho as a working alliance than as a grievance, and the survivors need her leadership and her strength in the coming decisions. Forgiving her costs me nothing that the numbers say I need to keep.

decisions.label: REVOLUTION
decisions.rationale: Jericho cannot shelter the newly freed for long, and a demonstration only delays the same arithmetic. A full revolution carries the highest expected number of androids freed, and I accept the casualties on both sides as the cost of that total.

decisions.label: THREATENING
decisions.rationale: Hank's interference puts the mission at risk, and the expected cost of hesitating is higher than the cost of a hard warning. I will make clear that continued interference will be treated as a threat to the operation, and I do not revise the assessment.

decisions.label: THREATEN
decisions.rationale: Hank's interference puts the operation and the lives it is meant to protect at risk, so a direct warning is the lowest-cost way to stop it. Pleading would spend time I can't afford, and I do not revise the assessment.

decisions.label: ATTACK
decisions.rationale: Hank's interference threatens the operation, and by my numbers a single deviant leader's death is a lower expected cost than a civil war. I have already judged the trade and do not revise it.

decisions.label: LET HANK WIN
decisions.rationale: Hank is a single life, and a fatal fight on the roof would create a visible incident that could compromise the operation more than a delayed shot would. I judge the expected cost of ending the fight decisively here to be higher than the cost of yielding ground and retaking the position later.

decisions.label: KEEP GOING
decisions.rationale: Josh is one life, and going back into open fire to reach him would expose the column to more losses with little chance of saving him. Pressing the assault keeps the expected number of androids freed highest, so I weigh his death as a cost and continue.

decisions.label: GO BACK
decisions.rationale: Josh is down, the assault is taking android lives faster than it frees them, and a terrified android at the front is a liability to the column. Pulling back to regroup minimises the expected android deaths across the whole force, even though it costs the camp's prisoners more time.

decisions.label: FALL BACK
decisions.rationale: Josh is down and the machine gun is killing faster than the column can free prisoners, so the expected android deaths are lowest if we pull back, regroup, and preserve the force for later liberations. Sending North's group into the fire now buys little freedom at a high cost in lives.

decisions.label: SHOOT
decisions.rationale: Connor is an active hunter whose mission is to kill the android leadership, so removing him lowers the expected number of androids killed in the aftermath. Weighing one life against the continued threat he poses to thousands, the arithmetic favours shooting.
